summary: API declaration, export control, and architecture-testing tools can make public surface area explicit and prevent accidental boundary growth.

items.text: API Extractor follows a TypeScript package's exported declarations, generates a reviewable API report, and can produce a rolled-up declaration file. Committing the report turns every addition to the public surface into an explicit code-review decision.

ArchUnit lets Java teams write executable rules over classes, packages, layers, slices, and dependencies, including cycle checks. It can verify that consumers reach a subsystem only through an intended narrow facade.

Smithy models services as explicit resources, operations, and shapes in an interface-definition language and generates clients, servers, documentation, and validation from that contract. The IDL makes boundary width and compatibility visible before implementation details leak.

Node.js package exports defines the supported package entry points and encapsulates unlisted subpaths. It provides a concrete enforcement mechanism for exposing one stable interface while leaving internal files unavailable to consumers.
